new_entities.name: Baby-led weaning
new_entities.description: A complementary feeding approach in which infants primarily self-feed hand-held foods rather than being spoon-fed purees.

new_entities.name: Growth outcomes
new_entities.description: Anthropometric outcomes such as weight gain, length or height gain, BMI z score, or overweight risk during infancy and early childhood.

edges.effect_quant: In the BLISS randomized clinical trial of 206 mother-infant pairs, a baby-led approach did not significantly change BMI z score at 12 or 24 months versus usual feeding, while a 2026 systematic review concluded that current growth evidence remains limited and inconsistent.
edges.population: healthy infants during complementary feeding, usually from around 6 to 24 months of age
edges.mechanism: Baby-led feeding may alter satiety responsiveness, food texture exposure, and energy self-regulation, but it can also vary widely in nutrient density and parental implementation.
edges.summary: Baby-led weaning does not show a clear consistent advantage or disadvantage for infant growth overall. The best current reading is mixed evidence with mostly neutral BMI or weight findings, but limited trial depth and implementation heterogeneity.
edges.caveats: BLW is not a single standardized protocol, and studies vary in how strictly self-feeding is implemented. Growth findings may differ depending on breastfeeding status, iron-rich food provision, and whether caregivers use a modified BLISS-style protocol.

evidence.citation: Marquez-Diaz RR et al 2026 Nutr Rev
evidence.notes: Baby-Led Weaning vs Traditional Spoon-Feeding: A Systematic Review of Infant Growth, Choking Risk, and Iron Status Among Infants Aged 6-12 Months.

evidence.citation: Taylor RW et al 2017 JAMA Pediatr
evidence.notes: Effect of a Baby-Led Approach to Complementary Feeding on Infant Growth and Overweight: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
